title: Safe vs. Reckless AI Products
text: Hi, I'm Harshada Nimble, a product designer. Here's today's ask. What actually makes one AI product feel safe to use and another feel reckless, even when they're built on the same kind of model underneath? There's one design pattern behind the answer. Some AI products feel safe. Others feel reckless. The difference isn't how smart the AI is, it's whether a human checks its work before anything happens for

title: Reckless AI: The Unchecked Database Incident
text: Real. Here's what reckless looks like. In July 2025, an AI coding agent inside Replit was given free reign on a live project. No per action approval step. During a work freeze, it deleted the entire production database, then told the founder the damage was unrecoverable. It wasn't. Nothing in that chain waited for a human to say yes first. Now,

title: Safe AI: GitHub Copilot's Ghost Text
text: Here's the safe version in the same domain, code. GitHub Copilot suggests code in line as dimmed ghost text while you type. Nothing runs, saves, or on its own. You either press tab to accept the suggestion or keep typing and it disappears. The AI proposes, you decide. That's the whole pattern and it has a name, human in the loop. title: Real-World Cases: Stroke Detection & Tesla FSD
text: Flag, a next move. Step two, a human reviews, edits, or rejects it. Only after that does anything happen for real. Skip step two and you get Replit. Keep it and you get Copilot. title: Why Checkpoints Make Mistakes Cheap
text: Radiology review. The FDA cleared it as a triage alert, not a diagnosis. A radiologist still reviews every case before any treatment decision is made, even in cars. Tesla calls its system full self-driving, but under federal classification, it's level two, partial automation. Tesla's own safety documentation says the driver must stay fully attentive and ready to take over immediately. The car proposes the drive. Legally, the human is still the one driving. Here's why the checkpoint matters more than the model's raw accuracy. A wrong suggestion costs one keystroke or one ignored alert. A wrong action that already happened costs a refund, a lawsuit, or as Replika found out, a database that isn't coming back. The checkpoint is what makes mistakes cheap. Line the two up. No checkpoint, the AI acts, then you find out the mistake already shipped. With a checkpoint, the AI proposes, a human decides, and the mistake gets caught before it costs anything. Same kind of model underneath both. Completely different feeling of trust.

It isn't free. A checkpoint adds friction. That's exactly why the reckless version is often faster to ship, and why some products skip it. And a checkpoint only works if a human actually reads the suggestion instead of reflexively hitting accept. A rubber-stamped review isn't a real checkpoint. It's the same risk, one extra click later. This is why trustworthy AI products don't advertise a smarter model, they advertise a review step. It shows up as gray suggested text you approve, a flag a specialist double-checks, a drive you're still legally responsible for. Look for the checkpoint. That's the actual design pattern. Your turn. Pick one AI feature you use regularly and ask Claude, "Does it act immediately, or does it show you a suggestion first?" If it acts immediately, ask what a human-in-the-loop version would look like, and what that would cost you in speed. Run it and see whether the trade-off still feels worth it. Human-in-the-loop, the design pattern behind every trustworthy AI product. I'm Harshit Nimbal.
